results.question: display a log of my most recent keystrokes, I did something weird and can't recall what
results.answer: Use the command `recent-keys` to display a log of your most recent keystrokes. This function returns a vector containing the last 300 input events from the keyboard or mouse [2] . If you want to see complete key sequences, use `recent-keys` with `include-cmds` non-nil. This will help you recall what you did recently. Note that if you've used a keyboard macro, those events are excluded, as they are less useful for debugging [2] . You can also use `C-h e` (view-echo-area-messages) to review recent echo area messages in Emacs [1] . However, `recent-keys` is the most direct method for viewing recent keystrokes. [2]

results.answer: Use `dired-compare-directories` in Emacs to compare two directories and mark differing files [1] . This command compares the current Dired buffer with another directory, highlighting files that differ in file names, size, modification time, or attributes. It can be customized with a Lisp expression for more stringent comparisons. For a command-line tool, `git-diff-tree` compares tree objects, but it is not designed for comparing arbitrary folders. Thus, the best-suited tool from the provided manual pages for comparing two folders and seeing which files differ is the Emacs `dired-compare-directories` command. [1]

have a template inserted automatically whenever I create a new file of a given type
results.answer: Yes, you can have a template inserted automatically whenever you create a new file of a given type using the `auto-insert-alist` variable in Emacs. When a file is created and is empty, Emacs checks `auto-insert-alist` to determine if a template should be inserted. Each entry in the list can match a mode or a file name regexp, and if a match is found, a predefined text or template is inserted [1] and [3] — this behavior is triggered when visiting a new empty file or when a file is created with a specific type. You can customize this behavior using `define-auto-insert` in your init file [3] to define templates for specific modes or file types. This is the mechanism for automatic template insertion based on file type. [1]

results.question: I want a second shell going but emacs keeps reusing the same one, can I give this one another name
results.answer: Yes, you can give a second shell a different name by using `M-x rename-uniquely` on the existing `*shell*` buffer, then running `M-x shell` again. This creates a new buffer named `*shell*` while the old one retains its new unique name. [3]

results.question: I want to search all the .c files under a folder for a string, what should I use
results.answer: Use `git-grep` with the pattern `*.c` if you are within a Git repository: `git grep 'string' -- '*.*'` [2] — but note that this searches tracked files in the working tree. For a general-purpose search across all `.c` files (not limited to Git), use `find` with `grep` as follows: `find . -name '*.c' -exec grep 'string' {} \;` [1] — this searches all `.c` files recursively and prints lines matching the string. The most direct and widely applicable tool is `find` combined with `grep`. [1]

results.answer: Yes, you can have the matching bracket highlighted when your cursor is next to one using the option `show-paren-highlight-openparen`. This option, when set to a non-`nil` value (i.e., enabled), highlights an open paren when point is just before it. Since this behavior applies to all delimiters (parentheses, braces, brackets), it will work for matching brackets as well [1] (and confirmed in [3] for periphery cases). The default is non-`nil`, so it is already enabled by default. Thus, highlighting occurs when the cursor is next to a matching bracket. [1]

results.question: how would I write a quick automated test for my elisp function
results.answer: Use the `ert-deftest` macro to define a test, include a docstring describing the test, and write Lisp code that calls your function with various inputs and compares the output to an expected value using `should` and `eql` or `equal`. For example: `(ert-deftest my-function-test () (should (equal (my-function "input") "expected")))` [3] and [4] . This approach formalizes comments with expected outputs and allows automated testing within Emacs. [4]

rename the document I'm editing so it is stored under a different name on disk
results.answer: Use `M-x rename-file` in Emacs to rename the document. This command renames the file on disk, and if the new name already exists, you must confirm with 'yes' [1] or the rename will not be performed. If the file and new name are on different file systems, the file is copied and then deleted [1] (this behavior is consistent with the `mv` command in Unix-like systems). For a direct command-line equivalent, use `mv` with the desired new name. For example: `mv oldname.txt newname.txt`. This will rename the file under a different name on disk [2] (note: `mv` is the standard command for renaming or moving files). If you are using Git, use `git mv` to rename a file within a Git repository [4]

results.question: use-package lazy load bind key
results.answer: The correct way to lazy-load a key binding in `use-package` is to use the `:defer t` keyword to delay loading the package until needed, combined with `:bind` to define the key binding. This ensures the package is not loaded immediately during startup, thus lazy-loading it, and the key binding is set up after the package is loaded. The binding itself is defined using the `:bind` keyword, and if the command is a keymap, use `:bind-keymap` instead [3] and [5] respectively. However, for standard function commands, `:bind` with `:defer t` achieves lazy loading of the key binding. Thus, the answer is: use `:defer t` with `:bind`. [4]

results.question: how do I pop up a clickable outline of sections for my latex paper, I keep forgeting where things are
results.answer: Use the command `C-c C-o C-e` to show the text content of a section, and `S-mouse-2` to hide it. results.question: how do I sotre a link to the place I'm at in my notes
results.answer: Use the `store-link` protocol with a bookmark. Add a bookmark named, for example, 'Org: store-link' with the location set to: `javascript:location.href='org-protocol://store-link?url=' + encodeURIComponent(location.href);`. When you click it, Emacs will store a link to the current location in your Org file. [5]

results.question: make every use-package declerations install missing packages automatically
results.answer: Use the `:ensure` keyword in every `use-package` declaration to automatically install missing packages. This ensures that if a package is not already present, it will be installed by the Emacs package manager. For a global default, set the user option `use-package-always-ensure` to a non-nil value, e.g., `(setq use-package-always-ensure t)` [1] and [4] . However, to meet the requirement of making *every* declaration install missing packages automatically, the explicit `:ensure t` should be used in each declaration. [1]
